Neonatal Asian elephants are among the largest terrestrial newborns, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 107,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 107,000 grams], a value that reflects the substantial investment required to produce a precocial calf capable of standing and walking shortly after parturition. Gestation in Elephas maximus is notably protracted, with a reported age at birth of 644 days [tg = 644 days] under the thermoneutral conditions typical of captive facilities in tropical climates (35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]). This extended gestational period, among the longest of any terrestrial mammal, is consistent with the slow life-history pace that characterizes large-bodied proboscideans. Following birth, the neonatal calf enters a period of exclusive lactation and maternal dependence, with weaning occurring at an average of 548 days since birth [tx = 548 days since birth] when maintained at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. The transition to nutritional independence is gradual, and calves often continue to nurse intermittently for several months beyond this point while learning to forage on their own.

As the calf grows, it undergoes a prolonged juvenile stage before reaching reproductive maturity. Longitudinal field records from wild populations in Sri Lanka and India indicate that the time since birth at puberty is 3,287 days [tp = 3,287 days] under conditions approximating 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], a threshold that reflects the extensive somatic development required before gonadal activation can occur. This delayed maturation is typical of megafaunal mammals and is accompanied by a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 65.5 years [am = approximately 65.5 years] at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], though free-ranging individuals rarely achieve this due to ecological constraints such as resource limitation and anthropogenic pressures. The combination of late puberty and extended longevity places Asian elephants among the slowest-living mammalian species, with generation times measured in decades rather than years. Comparative analyses with African savanna elephants reveal broadly similar developmental trajectories, although subtle differences in maturation timing have been documented across subspecies.

Body size metrics for adult Elephas maximus have been estimated from extensive field measurements of free-ranging individuals across the species range. The ultimate shoulder height of a fully grown male can reach approximately 270 centimeters [Li = approximately 270 centimeters], placing it among the tallest extant terrestrial mammals, though females typically attain slightly lower stature. This impressive vertical dimension is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 3,178,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,178,000 grams], a value estimated from relative allometric comparisons with Loxodonta africana and confirmed through opportunistic weighings of captive animals. Such immense body mass imposes substantial metabolic demands, even at rest. The peak food intake required to sustain an adult at maximum size has been recorded at 150,000 grams per day  when foraging under ambient conditions of 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C], a rate that reflects the enormous daily energy turnover needed to maintain homeostasis in a megathermic endotherm operating in hot, humid tropical environments.

Reproductive output in the Asian elephant is correspondingly modest, as predicted by life-history theory for a species of its body size. The maximum daily reproduction rate, derived from field observations, is approximately 0.00055 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 0.00055 offspring per day] at 35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]. Expressed in natural terms, females typically produce a single calf per reproductive event [N_R_i = single calf per reproductive event], with an interbirth interval corresponding to approximately 2 to 3 events per decade [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 events per decade]. This low fecundity is partially offset by high calf survival under favorable conditions, though poaching and habitat fragmentation have depressed recruitment rates across much of the species' range. The wet weight at weaning, estimated at 400,000 grams [Wwx = 400,000 grams], represents a nearly fourfold increase over birth mass and underscores the substantial maternal energetic investment during the lactation period. Mothers continue to provide nutritional and social support well beyond weaning, with calves often remaining in close association with the maternal herd for several additional years.

Puberty in free-ranging Elephas maximus populations, as documented through long-term observational studies of known individuals, occurs at approximately 9 years after birth [tp = approximately 9 years after birth] under thermoneutral conditions (35.8 °C [T = 35.8 °C]), corresponding to the 3,287-day threshold noted earlier. This late onset of reproductive maturation, combined with the 22-month gestation period, constrains the lifetime reproductive output of females to relatively few calves over their extended lifespan. Management strategies for this endangered species must therefore prioritize the protection of adult females and their offspring, as the demographic resilience of Asian elephant populations depends critically on the survival of reproductively active individuals over many decades.
